titre: Oil industry data rediscovered a drowned country
accroche: Trawlers have been hauling mammoth tusks out of the North Sea for a century. That ground once carried hunter-gatherers, before it was drowned
contenu_vulgarise:
Trawlers dragging the floor of the North Sea have long brought up mammoth tusks and flint tools caught in their nets, from tens of meters down. These objects do not come from a shipwreck; they come from ground that once carried hunter-gatherers, before it was swallowed by the sea.

Archaeologists call this now-submerged plain between England, the Netherlands, and Denmark Doggerland. Until the 2000s, its extent could only be guessed from isolated finds. To really see it, data had to be borrowed from an industry that has nothing archaeological about it.

## Oil data read another way

Oil companies map the seabed with reflection seismology: they send sound waves into the ground and record their echoes to locate rock layers that might contain oil. What these surveys also show, though no one was looking for it, are the traces of a landscape buried under marine sediment: riverbeds, valley slopes, wetlands.

In the early 2000s, the archaeologist Vince Gaffney and his team, then at the University of Birmingham, obtained from the company Petroleum Geo-Services a first batch of 6,000 square kilometers of seismic data from the Dogger Bank. The company later supplied another 19,000. By reconstructing these surveys layer by layer, the team brought back the course of vanished rivers, marshes, hills, a whole landscape that had remained invisible under tens of meters of water and mud.

## What the end of the story also reveals

The image that circulates is that of a cataclysm, an immense wave that supposedly swallowed Doggerland all at once, about 8,150 years ago, when a section of the Norwegian continental slope collapsed and set off the Storegga tsunami.

A study published in 2020 in the journal Antiquity qualifies this account. By the time of the tsunami, Doggerland was no longer the vast original Mesolithic plain: the rise in sea level, slow and continuous for millennia, had reduced it to a residual sandbank, Dogger Island. Depending on local terrain, the wave struck some areas head-on and spared others, sheltered by that same bank. Part of the coastline would thus have survived for more than a thousand years after the tsunami.

The disappearance of Doggerland is therefore not the story of a single instant. It is that of a retreat lasting several millennia, punctuated by a violent event, but not completed by it.

repere.texte: 3D seismic data from the Dogger Bank show that a system of meandering rivers occupied the emerged plain, replaced by a network of channels before the sea submerged the bank, around 7,500 years before present.
repere.source: Fitch, Thomson & Gaffney, “Late Pleistocene and Holocene depositional systems and the palaeogeography of the Dogger Bank, North Sea,” Quaternary Research, 64 (2), 2005, pp. 185-196

carte.punch: Data designed to find oil rediscovered a vanished country
carte.idee: Beneath the North Sea lies Doggerland, a plain where hunter-gatherers lived before it was submerged. Archaeologists reused oil-industry seismic surveys to recover its layout, with its rivers, valleys, and wetlands, which had remained invisible under tens of meters of water.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: Hakai Magazine, “Conjuring the Lost Land Beneath the North Sea”
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: In English. A detailed account of the collaboration between archaeologists and the oil industry.

quiz.question: What does the 2020 study really change about the Storegga tsunami and Doggerland?
choix: It proves the Storegga tsunami never reached the coasts of Doggerland
It shows that the submersion was already due to rising sea levels before the tsunami
It demonstrates that Doggerland was never inhabited by human populations
It establishes that oil-industry seismic data had until then been unusable
quiz.explication: The tsunami did strike, and unevenly depending on the terrain, but most of the submersion already came from a sea-level rise under way for millennia: the tsunami did not swallow Doggerland all at once; it punctuated a disappearance already in progress.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where did the data that made it possible to map the drowned landscape of Doggerland come from?
choix: From seismic surveys made by oil companies looking for oil
From direct archaeological dives carried out in the 2000s
From glacier ice cores taken in Greenland
From aerial photographs of the North Sea taken since the 1950s
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Oil companies map the seabed with reflection seismology to locate rock layers that might contain oil, and these surveys also revealed, though no one had been looking for it, the traces of the buried landscape.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How many square kilometers of seismic data did Petroleum Geo-Services supply to Vince Gaffney's team in total?
choix: 6,000 square kilometers, in a single batch
100,000 square kilometers, in five successive batches
2,000 square kilometers, taken only around the Dogger Bank
25,000 square kilometers, in two batches of 6,000 and then 19,000
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Vince Gaffney's team obtained a first batch of 6,000 square kilometers of seismic data from the Dogger Bank, and the company later supplied another 19,000, for a total of 25,000 square kilometers.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the study published in 2020 in Antiquity, what had Doggerland become just before the Storegga tsunami?
choix: An intact plain, as vast as at the start of the Mesolithic
An area already entirely submerged for several millennia
A residual sandbank, Dogger Island, no longer the vast original plain
A densely populated region of farming villages
quiz_supplementaire.explication: At the time of the tsunami, the sea-level rise, slow and continuous for millennia, had already reduced Doggerland to a residual sandbank, Dogger Island, and no longer the vast original Mesolithic plain.
